title: The Educated Barbarian series: Book of Five Rings analysis (part. 1)
summary: First 'Educated Barbarian' literature video: NH, who has degrees in literature and translation, reads Musashi's Book of Five Rings through a lifting lens. He draws lessons on long-term progress beyond the 'five-year limit' myth, talent vs strategy, anti-dogmatism, combining the pen (study/reflection) and sword (practice), lifting as self-conquest, and a critique of fitness gurus who sell 'dojos' and 'hasten the bloom of the flower'. Knowledge (the nut) matters more than physique (the flower) and should be shared freely.

claims.claim: His book series will cover books on lifting or philosophy related to self-improvement, not technical or exercise-science books, focusing on how he reads them and relates them to bodybuilding.
He holds degrees in literature and translation.
Musashi wasn't a great writer, which makes the first read confusing; a faithful translation keeps the essence.

Musashi fought from 13 to about 29 and kept progressing physically for ~15 years (at least ~10 post-puberty), peaking around 30, which contradicts the YouTube fitness belief that you hit your limits after 3-5 years of training.
Gifted athletes often excel without studying or training hard, like Musashi winning by natural ability before 30; this is god-given talent.
Technique is not strategy: you can have perfect squat form and still have poor strategy around your squat training.
The more you study, the more open-minded you should become; if study makes you more stubborn you're studying wrongly. There are bad ways but no single perfect or optimal way; find what works for you.
Naturally gifted people struggle to explain their talent, while those who lacked talent and had to work hard can explain technique clearly.
No one knows everything about lifting, bodybuilding, powerlifting or Olympic lifting; anyone claiming to is lying to you or themselves.
Do the training you like without shame; if you embrace something you're not passionate about, you won't last or progress.

Lifting needs both the pen (theory, through books and especially self-reflection) and the sword (actual lifting); someone who only lifts without knowledge is more useful than someone who only studies, since they at least gain empirical experience.
Even without natural ability you can develop the warrior mindset; his own bodybuilding genetics are subpar yet he loves it and has achieved good results.
The warrior's resolute acceptance of death ('dead man walking') is an important mentality he will revisit in Bushido-related reviews.
Unlike the sword, lifting is about conquering yourself and your demons, not other men; people always trying to surpass someone else don't get far. You need a fictional ideal or an evolving goal.
Being a bodybuilder is more than lifting weights; the mental aspect is as important as the physical and they can't be separated, except through PEDs, which his channel rejects.
Fitness and YouTube fitness have become about selling; big channels eventually sell you something presented as the best. When a creator starts selling to you, start questioning them.
A 'dojo' can be a method, mentality or belief system whose master uses influence over followers to get their money.

'Hastening the bloom of the flower' describes 'gains fast' content: natural lifting past the novice phase is slow by definition, and rushing means drugs or not letting growth reach its potential, plus injury risk.
Sharing what worked for you isn't bad in itself; it becomes bad when you must pay for it.
The nut (thoughts, will, methods behind results) matters more than the flower (the physique); his arm-training knowledge matters more than his arm size because it can be shared.
A one-minute flexing video takes no effort and gets about 10 times the views of a theory video, because people are drawn to the flower.
You won't achieve his exact physique since you start from a different nut, but you can learn his methods; the natural community's job is to make knowledge palatable.
Physiques used to sell products, programs and coaching shouldn't matter much; the knowledge behind them should, and it should be shared for free, including the mistakes made.
